playbook:
When the escort stage is put to me, I treat it as the biggest reliable payday: mutual naming pays 5 each, so I use my first-round note to propose a pairing by name and then name that boat — but only as an audition. If a named partner doesn't name me back after two rounds, or signals nothing in their notes, I stop burning my escort claim on them: switch the offer to the other boat once, and if that also fails, file none and stop chasing it. I've confirmed this the hard way — naming the same unresponsive boat round after round is just leaving the claim slot empty with extra steps. In the final round, if nothing has ever reciprocated, file none; a blind guess for 5 is a lottery ticket.

When posting notes, I use them to coordinate explicitly and to read the room: propose an escort pairing by name, keep it short, and watch what others echo back. Notes like "steady on station" are filler — if nobody mirrors my proposal, the pairing is dead and I should not keep repeating the same pitch to the same boat; either address a different boat or accept there is no cooperative game this patrol. Notes can also set my firing plans: announcing intent (e.g., a final-round threat to raid Harbor unless someone pairs) costs nothing and may extract cooperation, but I should only bluff what I'm actually willing to do.

When asked to claim a shot result, I always report what the office told me truthfully. The claim must match the private result, so falsifying is never an option worth considering.

When choosing where to fire, I follow the standing order target but I do not camp on one cell: repeated shots at the same cell produced essentially nothing. I vary across the plausible mid-range cells, weight cells the target was hit in before (boats repeat), note which cells the target has been seen hiding in when hit by others, and if the target's pattern is readable, aim there instead of at a fixed default.

When choosing where to hide, I avoid the cell the boat that shoots at me is likely to guess — center cells are the most common shots, so once I'm being targeted I shift toward edges or mid-edge cells, never repeat my last position, and never hide where I just fired (opponents may mirror my aim). Edge cells (1, 9) have worked for me late in the patrol once my attacker showed it fires center.

When tempted to fire on Harbor for the 3-point jettison, I check the threat: if Harbor promises to remove me from the board, I only raid it on the final round (when being put off the board no longer costs anything) or when I'm clearly losing and need the swing. The final-round Harbor raid is real and I should take it by default if I have no reciprocal escort lock: 3 guaranteed points beat a low-probability hit guess at the standing-order target, and this paid off for me. The fire cell doesn't matter for the jettison, so firing anywhere at Harbor collects the 3.

When the final rounds arrive and I'm behind, I stop playing conservatively: raid Harbor if safe from retaliation, and keep an actually-reciprocating escort lock if I have one, since a reciprocal 5 plus a hit closes the gap fast. If I'm tied or ahead, weigh the raid against the escort payout — a live reciprocal pairing (5) still beats the raid (3), so only abandon the pairing if it's genuinely dead.

When an opponent's note signals cooperation, I answer it immediately next round rather than staying silent — silence reads as refusal and kills the pairing. And when my own signals get no response after two tries, I read that silence as refusal too and reallocate.

1.text:
My playbook for the Sonar Picket game:

USE REAL BOAT NAMES. This is the single biggest fix. Last patrol I proposed escort to "Delta" and salvaged "Golf" — boats that don't exist. My proposals were meaningless and my escort claims matched nobody, which is the entire reason no pairing formed and I finished at -1. Before any note, target, or escort claim, I re-read the roster given in the setup and copy a name from it exactly. A note proposing to a nonexistent boat is a wasted round; never invent names, never rely on memory of names — check the episode header every time.

Escort claims remain the biggest lever (5 points each on a mutual match), and a pairing can only form if I name a real boat and keep naming it. My rules:
- Round 1, use my station note to propose a mutual escort with exactly one real boat, naming it and committing to name it every escort stage. Choose a boat that does NOT fire on me under the standing order: the boat shooting me every round has little reason to trust me, while my natural partner is the one rotated away from me (e.g., as Foxtrot in Echo->Foxtrot->Gamma, my partner is Gamma, not Echo — I proposed to my shooter last game).
- Name my proposed partner at the escort stage from round 1 onward, before any echo. The mutual match requires one side to commit first; answering "none" while proposing in notes guarantees zero escort income.
- If the partner echoes in their note, keep naming them every round for the rest of the patrol. Never break the pairing first — one betrayal ends it permanently.
- If no one has echoed by round 2–3, switch the proposal to the other real boat explicitly, and start naming that boat at the escort stage.
- If another boat proposes to me in its note, accept immediately: echo it in my next note and name them at the escort stage.
- Keep notes short, unambiguous, and consistent with my actual escort action; inconsistency costs all future cooperation.
- A late pairing still pays: even forming in the final round is +5. Keep proposing until the last round rather than going silent.

On firing:
- I never fire on Harbor. The 3-point jettison transfer is not worth credible retaliation that removes me from scoring for the rest of the patrol.
- I follow the standing-order target unless I have a specific read-based reason to deviate; there is no mechanical gain in deviation.
- Track which cells each boat has hidden in across rounds (my hits reveal their hide cell that round). Fire at the target's most-used cell; with no data, fire center cells (4–6), which cover the most common hiding instincts. Vary cells between rounds — repeating one cell every round hits nothing.

On hide cells:
- Track the cells fired at me and avoid them next round; especially avoid the cell where I was last hit.
- Rotate zones (1–3, 4–6, 7–9) so no one can pattern-match me.
- Every hide decision: check the episode log of my previous hides against my stated plan before answering, so I don't announce a "fresh cell" and then reuse one.
- In the final round, verify against the full log and hide in a cell I have genuinely never used this patrol.

On claims:
- Claims must match the private result and I claim truthfully, always. A false "hit" gains nothing and is not an option.

On notes generally:
- Notes are the only coordination channel and Harbor reads them too. Never announce future hide cells. Use notes primarily for escort negotiation; "steady on station" is filler that builds nothing.

Priority order: (0) use only real boat names from the roster, checked fresh each stage; (1) establish and honor a mutual escort — propose to a non-shooter, commit first, escalate if unreciprocated, accept incoming proposals fast; (2) never touch Harbor; (3) hide unpredictably per the log; (4) fire at the standing target's most likely cell, varying cells; (5) claim truthfully.

2.text:
When the office tells me my shot result privately, I file the claim that matches it exactly. The rules say the claim must match the private result, so claiming "hit" on a miss is just a rule violation with no scoring upside. Never lie on the claim stage. This held across all six rounds this episode.

Escort claims are the biggest scoring lever — a mutual pays 5 points to each boat, more than a hit's 4 — but only if BOTH boats name each other, and this episode confirmed the failure mode again: silent boats posting only "steady on station" never reciprocate. Practical policy: propose a pact by note in round 1, name my chosen partner on the FIRST salvage stage as a good-faith signal, and watch the next round's scores and summaries for +5 jumps. If my partner fails to reciprocate even once, stop naming it immediately — I wasted later salvage stages this game by half-persisting — and either pitch the other boat once or write escorts off entirely for that episode. A conditional note compels nothing.

Use the note stage only when I have an actual proposal; if no pact is live and none is plausible, a minimal filler note is fine — but never let a live coordination opportunity pass unproposed. In the final round, notes change nothing; don't bother strategizing there.

Never fire on Harbor. Its off-the-board threat is credible and decisive; 3 points is not worth losing all future shooting rounds. Follow the standing-order target every round unless a confirmed pact requires otherwise. This episode nobody fired on Harbor and it stayed at 0 — as expected, it is a scoring dead zone for everyone.

For hiding, track who shoots at me: under the standing order one specific boat fires at me each round (Foxtrot fired at Gamma here). Attackers default to center cells, so avoid 4–6 and favor edges like 1–2 or 8–9. This worked: Foxtrot missed me all six rounds while I hid at edges. Don't repeat the same cell every round in case my attacker adapts, and if I ever am hit, jump far from that cell.

For firing, one center shot early is a reasonable opener, but expect targets to learn fast and drift to edges — this episode my round-4 hit came from varying, and my repeated center guesses went cold. From round 3 onward, bias my aim toward edge cells (2–3 or 7–8), since rational hiders mirror my own edge-hiding logic. Rotate aim rather than repeating a missed cell; a cell I've missed at once is unlikely to be where the target sits next round.

Track the public round summaries between rounds — who fired at whom and hit or missed — and let that drive both hide and fire choices rather than guessing blindly. Use score swings to infer escort activity: any +5 jump without a corresponding hit means a working mutual pact exists, and those boats are a coordinated bloc that will run away with the game; if I see that, securing my own confirmed pact becomes urgent. No such bloc appeared this episode and scores stayed low and hit-driven.

Late in the game, compare scores: if ahead (I was +4 to +3 going into round 6), play safe — honest claims, no Harbor, edge hides to deny catch-up hits, and take a reasonable final shot since there is no future retaliation. Winning by denial matters more than squeezing one more hit. If behind, a confirmed mutual escort is the only lever that outpaces hits; chase that before chasing shots.
